text: Contrastive learning is the most common way to do it for representations: take two things that should mean the same (two augmentations of one image, an image and its caption, a sentence and its paraphrase), pull their embeddings together, and push them away from everything else in the batch.
label: core
key: two views of the same thing must land close

text: The pairing itself is the label; nobody annotates anything.
label: core

text: The parent page compares this paradigm with supervised training at one-screen level and shows that its loss is cross entropy again ( Topic: ml-fundamentals , Reading tab: "Beyond one network", and thread 1, "Everything is cross entropy").
label: core

text: The pairing is the label Before contrastive learning, self-supervision meant inventing a pretext task whose answer the data already holds: tell surrogate classes apart, where each class is one image under many transformations ( Dosovitskiy et al.
label: depth

text: 2014 ); predict where a second patch sits relative to the first ( Doersch et al.
label: fat

text: 2015 ); solve a jigsaw puzzle of tiles ( Noroozi and Favaro 2016 ); recognise which 2-D rotation was applied ( Gidaris et al.
label: depth

text: Each task was a proxy, and the features were good only insofar as the proxy happened to need them.
label: depth

text: Instance discrimination ( Wu et al.
label: fat

text: 2018 ) turned the proxy into the goal: treat every image as its own class, store each image's feature in a memory bank rather than in a classifier's weights, and use noise-contrastive estimation to cope with a million classes.
label: core

text: From there the target is the geometry itself: views of one thing close, different things apart.
label: core
key: made the geometry itself the goal

text: The geometry has older roots: a margin loss that pulls similar pairs together and pushes dissimilar pairs apart only while they are closer than a radius ( Hadsell, Chopra and LeCun 2006 ), and FaceNet's triplet loss, which separates a matching pair from a non-matching face by a margin ( Schroff et al.
label: core

text: Both compare one pair or triplet at a time; InfoNCE compares one positive against many negatives at once.
label: core
key: against all the negatives at once

text: InfoNCE, the workhorse loss L i = −log exp(sim( z i , z i + ) / τ) Σ k =1..
label: core

text: N exp(sim( z i , z k ) / τ) z i the anchor's embedding; z i + its positive; the sum runs over the positive and the N − 1 negatives sim cosine similarity, the dot product of l2-normalised vectors, so every logit lies in [−1/τ, 1/τ] τ the temperature, a fixed hyperparameter or (in CLIP) learned It is the softmax cross entropy of an N -way classification whose classes are the candidates in the batch and whose right answer is the positive ( van den Oord et al.
label: core

text: The cross-entropy view is on the parent page and on Loss functions ; temperature as a softmax knob is on Activation functions .
label: core

text: What is special here follows from three facts.
label: fat

text: 1 · The gradient goes where the softmax puts its mass Write s ij for the cosine between anchor i and candidate j and p ij for the softmax over s ij /τ.
label: core
key: The gradient goes where the softmax puts its mass

text: Differentiating the loss gives derived : ∂ L i /∂ s ij = ( p ij − 1[ j is the positive]) / τ The positive is pulled up by (1 − p positive )/τ and each negative is pushed down by p ij /τ; the pushes add up to the pull.
label: core
key: the pushes add up to the pull

text: So the negatives are not treated alike: each is pushed in proportion to how similar it already is, softmax-weighted.
label: core
key: in proportion to how similar it already is

text: The temperature sets how sharply: as τ falls, the weight concentrates on the hardest negatives; as τ rises, every negative gets the same small push.
label: core
key: as τ falls the push concentrates

text: Wang and Liu (2021) call this the hardness-aware property: "the temperature τ controls the strength of penalties on hard negative samples".
label: core

text: Too low a temperature also pushes apart things that genuinely belong together, their "uniformity-tolerance dilemma".
label: core

text: SimCLR's ImageNet sweep found τ = 0.1 best of {0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1} at batch 4,096 ( Chen et al.
label: core

text: 2020 , Table 5), 0.5 best on CIFAR-10 (Appendix B); SimCSE uses 0.05 ( Gao et al.
label: core

text: 2021 , Table D.1); CLIP learns it, starting from 0.07 and capping the logit scale at 100 (see the CLIP paper page).
label: core

text: See it on real data: the One real batch tab runs this loss on 48 real sentence pairs, with sliders for τ and the batch size, and shows for any anchor what share of the push its hardest negative takes.
label: fat
note: pointer to the removed One real batch tab; the lab is now inline

text: At SimCSE's τ = 0.05 the hardest negative alone takes 44% of the push on average after contrastive training (20% before); at τ = 1 it takes 3%, close to an even split of 1/47.
label: core

text: The CLIP paper page has the complementary toy: a tiny CLIP's 8 × 8 similarity matrix, live, where you can swap captions.
label: depth

text: 2 · The batch is the task A model that knows nothing puts probability 1/ N on the positive and scores ln N , so the batch size changes the task itself, not only the gradient noise (the parent page's correction makes the same point).
label: core
key: the batch size changes the task itself

text: CPC proves that the loss bounds the mutual information between the two views from below: I ≥ ln N − L , "which becomes tighter as N becomes larger" (§2.3).
label: core
key: which becomes tighter as N becomes larger

text: The bound can never exceed ln N ( Poole et al.
label: core

text: 2019 : "upper bounded by log K", with K the batch size), so ln 4,096 = 8.3 nats is the most a SimCLR batch can certify derived .
label: core

text: Correction to the old page "Maximises a lower bound on mutual information" is true but often over-read.
label: core

text: The bound is capped at ln N , it is loose when the true information is larger, and later work credits InfoNCE's success to the geometry it produces (next section) rather than to information it measures ( Wang and Isola 2020 ).
label: core
key: The bound is capped at ln

text: Also, in SimCLR each anchor has 2( N − 1) negatives, not N − 1: both augmented views of every other image count ("we treat the other 2(N−1) augmented examples within a minibatch as negative examples", §2.1).
label: core
key: augmented examples within a minibatch as negative examples

text: Hence the engineering that buys negatives: Big batches.
label: core

text: SimCLR trains at batch 4,096 by default and sweeps 256 to 8,192 (§2.2); CLIP uses 32,768 ( Radford et al.
label: core

text: A memory bank of every image's last-seen feature (Wu et al.
label: core

text: 2018): many negatives, but stale ones, computed by older versions of the encoder.
label: core

text: A queue with a momentum encoder (MoCo, He et al.
label: core

text: 2019 ): keys come from a second encoder whose weights are a moving average of the query encoder's, so the queue stays consistent; K = 65,536 keys, momentum m = 0.999 ("works much better than a smaller value"), τ = 0.07.
label: core
key: works much better than a smaller value

text: The number of negatives no longer depends on the batch.
label: core
key: no longer depends on the batch

text: A sigmoid instead of the softmax.
label: core
key: a sigmoid instead of the softmax

text: SigLIP scores every image-text pair as an independent binary decision, so the loss "does not require a global view of the pairwise similarities for normalization" ( Zhai et al.
label: core
key: does not require a global view

text: 2023 ); the CLIP paper page animates softmax against sigmoid on one batch.
label: core

text: 3 · Negatives are sampled, so some are wrong Random negatives include items that share the anchor's meaning or class, and the loss pushes them away anyway.
label: core

text: (2020) correct the objective for these false negatives ; Robinson et al.
label: core

text: (2021) go the other way and sample hard negatives on purpose, with a knob for how hard.
label: core
key: with a knob for how hard

text: The real batch has a natural false negative: "A woman is dancing in the rain." and "A man and woman are dancing in rain." are separate pairs, so each is the other's negative.
label: core
key: A man and woman are dancing in rain.

text: Both problems measured on a real retrieval corpus (how often a mined "negative" is really relevant on SciFact, and a positive-aware filter) are on Embedding models , sections 4 and 5.
label: core

text: The SimCLR recipe, which most image methods inherit SimCLR (Chen et al.
label: core
key: the recipe most image methods inherit

text: 2020) names the loss NT-Xent ("normalized temperature-scaled cross entropy") and finds three things matter.
label: core

text: Augmentation: "the combination of random crop and color distortion is crucial" (§3).
label: core
key: random crop and color distortion is crucial

text: A projection head: a small MLP g maps the representation h to the z the loss sees; a nonlinear head beats a linear one by about 3% and no head by more than 10% (§4.2), and after training "we throw away the projection head" and use h .
label: core
key: we throw away the projection head

text: Scale: large batches and long training.
label: core

text: Linear evaluation on ImageNet reaches 69.3% top-1 with a ResNet-50 and 76.5% with a ResNet-50 four times wider, "matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50"; fine-tuned on 1% of the labels it reaches 85.8% top-5 (Table 6 and abstract).
label: core

text: Correction SimCLR's often-quoted 76.5% is for ResNet-50 (4×), a network with four times the width; the plain ResNet-50 gets 69.3%.
label: core

text: And the 1%-label result, 85.8%, is top-5 accuracy, not top-1.

section: alignment and uniformity: what the loss actually builds
text: Alignment and uniformity: what the loss actually builds Wang and Isola (2020) split what InfoNCE optimises on the unit hypersphere into two measurable properties, and show that as the number of negatives grows the loss optimises exactly these two: ℒ align = E ( x , y ) positive ‖ f ( x ) − f ( y )‖ 2 ℒ uniform = log E x , y e −2‖ f ( x ) − f ( y )‖ 2 align positives should land close: lower is better, 0 when the two views coincide uniform all embeddings should spread over the sphere: lower is better; 0 when every point is the same (the exponent is then 0 for every pair) α, t the exponents 2 and 2 are the paper's defaults ( lalign(x, y, alpha=2) , lunif(x, t=2) ) The numerator of InfoNCE rewards alignment and the denominator rewards uniformity, and "directly optimizing for these two metrics leads to comparable or better performance than contrastive learning" (abstract).
label: core

section: alignment and uniformity: what the loss actually builds
text: Seen this way, collapse is not mysterious: alignment alone is minimised perfectly by mapping everything to one point, and only the uniformity half stops it.
label: core
key: only the uniformity half stops it

text: Asymmetry: BYOL and SimSiam BYOL ( Grill et al.
label: fat

section: without negatives: collapse and the defences against it
text: 2020 ) uses "two neural networks, referred to as online and target networks".
label: core
key: referred to as online and target networks

section: without negatives: collapse and the defences against it
text: The online network has an extra predictor MLP and is trained to predict the target network's projection of the other view; the target network gets no gradient and is an exponential moving average of the online weights, with rate starting at τ base = 0.996 and increased to 1 on a cosine schedule (§3.3). "While state-of-the art methods rely on negative pairs, BYOL achieves a new state of the art without them": 74.3% ImageNet linear top-1 with a ResNet-50 and 79.6% with a larger ResNet.
label: core

section: without negatives: collapse and the defences against it
text: SimSiam ( Chen and He 2020 ) strips BYOL down: no moving average, one shared encoder, a predictor on one branch and a stop-gradient on the other. "A stop-gradient operation plays an essential role in preventing collapsing": removing it alone drops ImageNet accuracy to 0.1%, and removing the predictor also fails (§4.1, §4.2, Table 1a).
label: core
key: plays an essential role in preventing collapsing

section: without negatives: collapse and the defences against it
text: To detect collapse the authors monitor the standard deviation of the l2-normalised output, which is about 1/√ d for spread-out outputs and 0 when collapsed.

text: Centering and sharpening: DINO DINO ( Caron et al.
label: core

section: without negatives: collapse and the defences against it
text: 2021 ) is self-distillation with no labels: a student network matches the softmax output of a momentum teacher (momentum following a cosine schedule from 0.996 to 1) across different crops.
label: core

section: without negatives: collapse and the defences against it
text: Two operations on the teacher's output prevent collapse, and each alone causes a different one: "centering prevents one dimension to dominate but encourages collapse to the uniform distribution, while the sharpening has the opposite effect" (§3.1).
label: core
key: centering prevents one dimension to dominate

section: without negatives: collapse and the defences against it
text: Centering subtracts a running mean of the teacher's outputs; sharpening uses a low teacher temperature, warmed up from 0.04 to 0.07 over the first 30 epochs, against 0.1 for the student.
label: core

section: without negatives: collapse and the defences against it
text: A centre that updates too slowly (momentum 0.999) collapses; 0.9 gave the best k -NN accuracy in the ablation (Appendix).

text: 2021 ) computes the cross-correlation matrix between the two views' embeddings over the batch and pushes it towards the identity: diagonal 1 (invariance), off-diagonal 0 (no redundancy between dimensions).
label: core

section: without negatives: collapse and the defences against it
text: VICReg ( Bardes, Ponce and LeCun 2021 ) separates the three jobs into three terms: invariance (mean squared distance between the views), variance (a hinge keeping each dimension's standard deviation over the batch above γ = 1) and covariance (off-diagonal covariances pushed to 0), weighted λ = μ = 25 and ν = 1.
label: core

text: These use the batch, but as a statistic, not as negatives; the variance hinge alone is what blocks the constant, and dropping it in the lab collapses the run to a single point after a few hundred steps, in all three seeds.

text: The trend the old page named still describes the field: the split is no longer "contrastive or not" but joint-embedding methods (contrastive, self-distillation, JEPA, which compare or predict embeddings) against masked generative methods (MAE, which reconstruct the input), with prediction in latent space increasingly favoured when the goal is semantic features.
